checks.setup:
A new pawn type, cloned from the working capsule prefab. Somewhere in the copy, `HasOwner` ends up unchecked on the ghost authoring component.

The pawn spawns on the server. It replicates to the client. You can see it, it is in the entity inspector on both sides, its transform is correct, and nothing anywhere logs a word.

It never moves. Not on the client, not on the server.
checks.ask: Trace it: what component is missing, which queries silently stop matching, and why does 'not on the client either' narrow it down so fast?
rightIf: says HasOwner is what adds the GhostOwner component to the ghost
concludes the movement system's WithAll<GhostOwner> filter now matches nothing, on both client and server
notes the input gather filter also fails, because GhostOwnerIsLocal is derived from GhostOwner matching your network id
explains the diagnostic value: failing on both sides means it is not a routing or wire problem — routing failures move the client and not the server
notes an empty query is not an error, which is why nothing is logged
checks.answer:
Without `HasOwner` there is no `GhostOwner` component, and `GhostOwner` is what two separate filters are keyed on. The movement system filters on it to decide what counts as a player-owned thing, so its query matches zero entities — on the client and on the server, identically, because it is the same system with the same filter running in both worlds. The input gather system filters on the local-owner tag, and that tag is added by NetCode when the owner id matches yours, so with no owner component there is nothing to match and nothing gets written either.

An empty query is not an error. It is a system doing nothing very efficiently, and DOTS will never tell you it happened.

The both-sides symmetry is the useful part of the evidence. A routing problem moves the client and not the server. A missing-schema problem shows up as the entity being absent on one side. Dead on both sides, with the entity present on both sides, points at a filter that matches nothing — and then you go and look at what the filters are keyed on.
checks.because: Ownership is a component, and a component that is not there is a query that matches nothing. Zero matches and correct behaviour look identical from the outside.

checks.setup:
Two players connect. Nerve spawns a persistent controller and a replaceable pawn for each, so the expected reading is:

    ClientWorld | conns=1 inGame=1 ghosts=4

You get `ghosts=3`. Both players can see each other, both capsules move, and the game appears entirely playable.
checks.ask: What does 3 mean specifically, what mechanism produced it, and what will go wrong later that has nothing to do with movement?
rightIf: counts the expected four as 2 controllers plus 2 capsules
concludes 3 means two connections adopted the same controller — one controller, two pawns
identifies the reconnect path as the mechanism: the spawn system looks for an existing controller with the same identity before creating one
names identity collision as the cause — two connections presenting the same AccountIdentity
predicts consequences on anything the controller owns: shared score, shared persistent state, and a respawn or disconnect that affects both players
checks.answer:
Four is 2 controllers plus 2 capsules. Three is one controller shared by two connections, and the mechanism that produced it is the reconnect path doing its job: before creating a controller the spawn system looks for an existing one with the same identity, because that is how a player who drops and rejoins keeps their score. Hand it two connections claiming the same identity and it will helpfully reunite them.

Movement is fine because movement lives on the pawn, and there are still two of those. Everything on the *controller* is now shared: score, unlocks, persistent identity, whatever accumulates across a life. One player's disconnect handling will reach into the other's session, and a respawn that re-points the controller's primary pawn will take the other player's body away.

This is the exact risk a synthetic local identity carries — a stopgap that derives the identity from something not actually unique will do this — and the four-ghost reading is what disproves it. That is why the count is worth checking rather than assuming: it is a value that cannot be right unless the mechanism you claim is working, worked.
checks.because: The controller is a stable device handle and the pawn is the currently mapped buffer. Two sessions on one handle is not a spawn bug, it is an identity bug that spawning faithfully executed.

checks.setup:
Respawn: the pawn is destroyed, a fresh capsule prefab is instantiated, the controller's primary-controlled link is re-pointed at it, and ownership is set. The new capsule appears in the right place and replicates.

The player cannot move it. The old capsule is gone — there is nothing left to move by mistake. The client is predicting the new capsule and it moves locally; the server's copy never does.
checks.ask: Which of the two routing mechanisms was updated and which was not, and what is the general rule the controller/pawn split implies?
rightIf: identifies that the controller link was re-pointed but the connection's CommandTarget still refers to the destroyed pawn
concludes commands arrive and are routed at a dead entity, so the server-side input never lands on the new capsule
notes the client predicts fine locally because it writes its own input component directly — the divergence is on the server side
states the rule: everything that names the pawn has to be updated when the pawn is replaced, not just the controller's own link
may note the automatic routing path avoids this by targeting ghosts you own rather than one fixed entity
checks.answer:
Two mechanisms point at a pawn and you moved one of them. The controller's primary-controlled link now names the new capsule; the connection's command target still names the destroyed one. Commands keep flowing and keep being delivered to an entity that no longer exists, so the server-side input for the new capsule stays at zero forever — the same signature as a pawn that never had routing at all.

The client looks fine because the client writes its input component locally and predicts from it. The whole failure lives on the server side of the wire, which is why "it moves on my screen" is not evidence that routing works.

The general rule falls out of why the split exists: the pawn is the replaceable half. Anything that names it by entity — command target, camera target, UI bindings, ability sources — is a pointer that becomes stale on every respawn, vehicle entry, and possession change. Either update all of them together in the one place that does the swap, or use the routing mechanism that targets *ghosts you own* rather than one specific entity, and let ownership do the addressing.
checks.because: The controller is the stable handle and the pawn is the mapped buffer. Re-mapping the buffer means re-pointing every pointer to it, not just the one you were thinking about.

checks.ask: What did Unity actually serialise onto that prefab, why, and what is the rule?
rightIf: says Unity only creates a MonoScript asset when the file name matches the class name
concludes there is no MonoScript for PlayerMoveInputAuthoring, so the component serialises with a null script reference
identifies the consequence: a component with no script is a component with no baker, so it contributes nothing at bake
notes nothing errors because a missing script is a normal serialised state Unity tolerates
states the rule: one MonoBehaviour per file, named after the file
checks.answer:
It serialised a component with a null script reference. Unity creates the `MonoScript` asset that a MonoBehaviour reference points at only when the class name matches the file name — so `PlayerMoveInputAuthoring` inside `PlayerMoveInput.cs` has no MonoScript to point at, and the prefab stores a script id of zero. The inspector shows a slot because the component entry exists; it shows nothing in it because there is no type behind it.

Downstream, that is a component with no baker, so baking produces nothing, so the capsule has no input component, so the gather system's query matches nothing and the movement system reads a component that is not there. Four layers of the stack behaving correctly on top of a script reference that is zero.

Nothing complains because a missing script is a state Unity handles routinely — you see it every time you delete a class. It is not an error, it is a shrug, and it shrugs all the way through your bake.

One MonoBehaviour per file, named after the file. Always.
checks.because: The prefab stores a pointer to a script asset, and the script asset only exists if the file name says so. A null pointer that Unity is comfortable with is a null pointer that bakes silently to nothing.
